newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ING still on U.S. hunt despite setback.
newsitem.headline: ING still on U.S. hunt despite setback.

text.p: ING Groep NV (ING), the Dutch financial services group with an estimated war chest of 7.5 billion guilders ($3.9 billion) for acquisitions, said on Thursday it would march on with plans to expand in the United States.

The banking and insurance group on Wednesday broke off talks to take over U.S. investment bank Dillon Read & Co, a decision analysts said was disappointing and a small setback to its goal of increasing its presence in U.S. securities markets.
But they also said a life insurance acquisition in the United States would remain the Dutch group's top priority.

ING withdrew from talks with the partners of privately-owned Dillon Read to buy the remaining 75 percent of the firm it does not already own, adding it expected the partners to exercise an option to buy ING's stake for an undisclosed price.
The Wall Street Journal earlier reported that Anglo-Swiss investment bank SBC Warburg wanted to buy Dillon Read for about $600 million, or three times book value.

ING spokesman Wieger Sietsma said the negotiations foundered on Dillon Read's wish to remain independent at a time when ING was integrating its worldwide corporate and investment banking units, including London-based merchant bank Barings.
But banking sources said price was also a sticking point as the partners, some of them corporate finance specialists, were also talking with other potential buyers.
Sietsma said ING had 1,200 investment banking staff in the United States, and the end of talks with Dillon Read did not change the strategy of growing its securities operations.
"What would be most useful is to have more distribution capacity in the U.S.," he said.
Heinie Hakker of BZW said Dillon Read may be seen as a missed opportunity, with ING's billion-guilder cash pile growing larger every day.
"They should, at a certain stage, do something with the money," he said, adding however that paying a high price for a company wanting to remain independent would not be positive.
Despite recent speculation linking ING with Wall Street firm Lehman Brothers, Hakker said he did not expect the group to look for a large target in U.S. investment banking.
"I don't think they're prepared to spend billions of guilders unless there's a golden opportunity," he said.
Kempen and Co analyst Hans Pluigjers saw the end of talks with Dillon Read as a "small setback" for ING in the short term, which may cost them some deals.
ING and Dillon Read, which specialises in mergers and acquisition work, have been co-operating for several years.
Pluigjers said however he believed ING could target firms ranked 15th to 30th among U.S. investment banks.
"It's much more interesting for them to buy medium-sized players with good distribution channels," he said.
He said ING could spend up to 7.5 billion guilders cash on acquisitions, and more if shares were offered to sellers.
Kishore Banger of Credit Suisse First Boston said it was positive ING was prepared to walk away from a deal that did not meet its strict internal guidelines on acquisitions.
He noted ING had shown a similar resolve when considering expansion in Belgian banking. "There's no need to rush. The market is peaking, globally, at the moment," Banger said.
Dennis Ederzeel of Delta Lloyd Bank said it was more important for ING to buy a U.S. life insurer because that sector was becoming more concentrated.
ING last year considered buying U.S. insurer First Colony, but it was sold to a rival bidder.
"ING has so much equity, almost anything is possible," he said.
